title: Putin Orders Russia's Army to 2.4 Million as the US Supreme Court Strikes Down Trump's Tariffs and Ethiopia Accuses Egypt and Sudan of Arming Tigray Rebels
subhead: Moscow signs its fourth military expansion this year, Washington's signature trade weapon is invalidated by its own top court, and a fresh Horn of Africa war pulls in regional rivals — three moves that reshape escalation, trade and alliance calculations at once.

sections.heading: Putin Orders a Fourth Expansion of Russia's Armed Forces This Year
sections.body:
Vladimir Putin signed a decree raising the authorized strength of the Russian armed forces to roughly 2.4 million personnel, including about 1.5 million active-duty troops, according to the Kyiv Post, Meduza and RBC-Ukraine. It is the fourth such expansion decree Putin has signed in 2026, a pace that signals the Kremlin is planning for a long war rather than a near-term settlement.

The decree drew little immediate detail on timelines or how the additional personnel would be sourced, and Ukraine's leadership responded by claiming Russia has already begun an additional mobilization wave (Kyiv Post). The announcement landed the same week Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones struck Kyiv, hitting civilian and academic sites including the National Academy of Sciences, killing at least seven people (CBS, Al Jazeera, Reuters).

Separately, Zelensky said North Korea is preparing to deploy another roughly 10,000 troops to Russia (Reuters), while Ukrainian intelligence alleged Moscow is expanding military cooperation with Pyongyang and sharing satellite intelligence with Iran on US and Gulf military sites (Kyiv Post).
sections.whyItMatters: A legally codified 2.4-million-man force is a structural commitment to sustained war, not a battlefield adjustment. Combined with the North Korea pipeline, it tells Kyiv and NATO that Russia is expanding its manpower base faster than sanctions or attrition are shrinking it.

sections.heading: US Supreme Court Invalidates Most of Trump's Tariffs
sections.body:
The US Supreme Court struck down the bulk of Trump's sweeping tariffs, ruling that the emergency-powers authorities used to impose them were illegal (ABC News, AP, CNN, Reuters). Reporting on the decision said Trump reacted sharply, calling the ruling a blow and vowing new levies by other means (AP).

The decision lands days after the US and China agreed to reciprocal tariff cuts on roughly $30 billion of goods following the Trump-Xi summit, with both sides publishing product lists and launching an AI dialogue (Al Jazeera, China Daily, Global Times). A separate WTO World Trade Report 2026 executive summary was also published this week, underscoring how much of the global trading system now hinges on unilateral US measures.

Trump also rolled back federal fuel-economy standards for automakers (ABC News, Washington Post), a move he argued will lower car prices while analysts disputed the claim.
sections.whyItMatters: The court has removed the legal foundation of Washington's main coercive trade instrument at a moment when tariff policy is the centerpiece of US leverage over China, Canada and the EU. The administration now has to rebuild its tariff architecture on firmer statutory ground — or lose the weapon the summit diplomacy was built around.

sections.heading: Ethiopia Accuses Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea of Arming Tigray Rebels
sections.body:
Ethiopia's army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Sudan, Egypt and other external powers of backing armed groups fighting federal forces in the north, saying the rebels could not make gains unless 'backed, supported and supplied' from outside (Al Jazeera). Sudan's military denied the allegations as 'baseless' and counter-claimed that the paramilitary RSF is receiving training, supplies and drone support from inside Ethiopian territory (Al Jazeera).

Fighting between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government resumed on Wednesday, raising fears of a return to the 2020-2022 civil war that killed an estimated 600,000 people (Al Jazeera). Ethiopian pro-government forces claimed the capture of a strategic Tigray town (Reuters), while a drone struck the headquarters of Tigrai TV in Mekelle and telecommunications in the region were disrupted, complicating reporting (Al Jazeera). UN chief Antonio Guterres said he was 'particularly troubled' by reports of drone use and civilian harm.
sections.whyItMatters: If Egypt and Sudan are genuinely supplying the TPLF, this becomes a proxy contest between Ethiopia and its Nile-basin rivals layered on top of a renewed civil war — threatening the stability of the Horn, the Nile dam dispute, and Red Sea security all at once. Even unverified, the accusation itself raises the risk of wider regional entanglement.

sections.heading: Netanyahu Makes Secret Trip to Abu Dhabi as Egypt Warns Surface
sections.body:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a previously undisclosed meeting with UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed in Abu Dhabi over the weekend, which the UAE confirmed via its state news agency (Reuters, Al Jazeera, AP). The Times of Israel reported, citing sources, that Netanyahu flew to the UAE to ask MBZ to deny a Haaretz report that the Emirati leader had warned him in advance of the Hamas attack; Netanyahu confirmed the visit but denied that request (Haaretz, Times of Israel). Israel's security agency filed a complaint over the TV report (SCMP).

The visit came as the Wall Street Journal reported that Egypt had warned Netanyahu of an impending attack on Israel before October 7, and as satellite imagery showed Israel continuing to expand into Gaza despite the ceasefire (NYT). The Palestinian death toll in the Gaza war has surpassed 74,000, according to Democracy Now!, while the UK pledged a tougher stance on Israeli actions in Gaza and the West Bank (Al Jazeera).
sections.whyItMatters: The trip shows the Abraham Accords channel being used for crisis management even as the Gaza war grinds on and Israeli domestic politics heat up before October's Knesset elections. If the October 7 warning claims harden, they become a domestic political weapon inside Israel and a strain on the very Gulf relationships Netanyahu is leaning on.

sections.heading: Yemen's Houthi-Saudi War Intensifies as the Conflict Reaches the Waterways
sections.body:
The renewed war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has killed more than 800 people, according to World Health Organization figures cited by the New York Times. Yemen's army said it killed or wounded 476 Houthis in 356 operations over 24 hours (Anadolu Ajansı), while Houthi officials accused Yemeni government forces of a deadly market strike; the government said it targeted a nearby Houthi military camp (DW, NBC).

The Houthis threatened to strike Saudi bridges and oil facilities if Riyadh escalates (Jerusalem Post, energynow.com). US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Saudi Arabia's foreign minister as the anti-Houthi campaign intensified (Al-Monitor). Analysts flagged that Houthi moves toward key waterways put regional shipping and the new Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact under strain (The Conversation, RFI).

On the energy front, Middle East oil exports have rebounded as Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz weakens, with Persian Gulf exports reaching about 72% of prewar levels (WSJ, New York Post), while Qatar-linked LNG traffic through Hormuz picked up (Reuters).
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthi-Saudi war is again the live maritime-risk story in the Red Sea corridor, even as Hormuz traffic recovers. Continued Houthi pressure on Saudi infrastructure and shipping lanes keeps insurance and rerouting costs elevated, and tests whether Riyadh's new regional defence partnerships actually deter strikes.

sections.heading: Serbia's Vučić Resigns Early to Run for Prime Minister
sections.body:
Serbia's longtime president Aleksandar Vučić resigned eight months before his term ended and will run for prime minister in October snap parliamentary elections (Guardian, Reuters, NYT, DW, France 24, Meduza). The move follows prolonged protests and reshapes a leadership that has tried to balance between the EU and Russia.

The resignation adds to a run of political turnover across Europe and the Balkans. In Germany, the far-right AfD's gains in the former East continue to dominate coalition calculations, while the EU is drafting a security protocol modelled on NATO's Article 4 to respond to Russian hybrid attacks (Politico, Daily Sabah). The Pentagon's policy chief said NATO allies back a shift toward European-led defence (Bloomberg), and Poland is fast-tracking a plan to build a 'small town' for US troops (TVP World).
sections.whyItMatters: Vučić has been a pivot between Moscow and Brussels; moving from the presidency to the premiership changes his mandate and the calculus around Serbia's EU path and its stance on Russia sanctions. It is another data point that Balkan and European domestic politics are becoming less stable as external pressure rises.

bottomLine: Three developments today each raise the stakes of a different contest. Putin's decree codifies a 2.4-million-man army, locking Russia into a long war. The US Supreme Court has gutted the legal basis of Trump's tariffs even as his administration touts a $30 billion tariff-cut deal with China — meaning Washington's core economic weapon must now be rebuilt or abandoned. And Ethiopia's charge that Egypt and Sudan are arming Tigray rebels risks turning a renewed civil war into a Nile-basin proxy fight. Meanwhile the Iran-Hormuz standoff continues in the background: talks are still alive via Qatar but stalled, oil flows are recovering toward prewar levels, and the Houthi-Saudi war has killed over 800 people. The through-line is that multiple conflicts are broadening their participants rather than narrowing toward settlement.
